messages.author: 791bfedbe5311275
messages.subject: Weighting a Bayesian model
parts:
Hello, 

I've read some other discussions about weighting a Bayesian model and it seems that weights are not really valid in a Bayesian sense. I don't understand why and I'm hoping someone can help me with the context of my problem. The situation I am modeling is crop yield. We are measuring yield from varying sizes of fields and would like to put more importance on larger fields. The crop experts' agree that larger fields provide a better estimate of yield and that information should be taken into account. If weights don't exactly make sense from the Bayesian perspective, is there an alternative way of incorporating this information, or could you help me with the intuition about why we don't need weights?

Many thanks!

messages.author: f53f4ca2c430170d
messages.subject: Re: Weighting a Bayesian model
parts:
On Friday, June 17, 2016 at 10:31:56 AM UTC-4, Brandon Whited wrote:
Hello, 

I've read some other discussions about weighting a Bayesian model and it seems that weights are not really valid in a Bayesian sense. I don't understand why and I'm hoping someone can help me with the context of my problem. The situation I am modeling is crop yield. We are measuring yield from varying sizes of fields and would like to put more importance on larger fields. The crop experts' agree that larger fields provide a better estimate of yield and that information should be taken into account. If weights don't exactly make sense from the Bayesian perspective, is there an alternative way of incorporating this information, or could you help me with the intuition about why we don't need weights?

Others have thought more about this but: assume the observation is yield/(m^2 of field), assume you observe only the field-level average yield/(m^2 of field) (or whatever resolution you have), build the model from there.  If one field1 is much larger than field 2, it will have more units where you measured yield in field1 and therefore show up more times in the likelihood. Then you add an observation model that says that you only observe the field-level sum and fit the whole thing in Stan. That's fully coherent but maybe difficult to fit b/c the field sub-unit parameters are going to be completely unidentified without further modeling (has within-field yield variation been quantified?)

 The ad-hoc weighting alternative is skip the observation model and just assume explicitly that the exact field1 observation appears multiple times based on how much bigger the field is.  That's wrong and mis-represents the variance of the field1 measurement but depending on the model there would be approximations that don't do such a rotten job of that.  I don't know that I've seen simulation studies that really get into this but we could do a Stan case study about it. 

That's the sketch... 

 

Many thanks!

messages.author: 1f723d378f24adbb
messages.subject: Re: [stan-users] Weighting a Bayesian model
parts:
If you believe that larger fields are measured with a proportionally
smaller variance, then with a relevant heteroskedastic model, it is as
if you weighted the data. See the "Unequal variances" in Chapter 14 of
BDA.

Best,

Tamas

messages.author: 8aa9b8cc06fdc99c
messages.subject: Re: [stan-users] Weighting a Bayesian model
parts:
It's just like Andrew's eight-schools example (where
you measure test score improvement with standard error
per school). The data is the measurement plus error.

The kinds of objections people have to weighting
is when it's something like adjusting for population
proportions and there's not a generative model behind
the data collection process.

- Bob
